claims.claim: Busy workers ≈ requests per second × time per request: at 40 req/s and ~450 ms that's about 18 sync workers busy at once (24 at 600 ms), against 17 workers
claims.measured: python-flask I/O wait (10 ms, 256 conns): 276 req/s, p50 915 ms
claims.why: The benchmark shows sync Flask behaving as if each worker holds one request (heavy queueing under I/O wait), but it doesn't give the worker count or a 200–600 ms upstream, so the 18-of-17 figure can't be checked.

claims.claim: With sync workers, if the insurer goes from 400 ms to 5 s, 17 workers can serve only about 3 requests a second
claims.measured: python-flask I/O wait (10 ms, 256 conns): 276 req/s at 18% CPU
claims.why: Low CPU and long queueing fit the one-request-per-worker model, but neither 17 workers nor a 5 s wait was measured.

claims.claim: A cancellation (short Postgres transaction in the Flask app) should finish in tens of milliseconds
claims.measured: python-flask single-row DB query at 64 conns: p50 41.54 ms, p99 57.99 ms, 1,529 req/s
claims.why: Even when saturated, sync Flask answers a single-query DB request in roughly 40–60 ms, which is tens of milliseconds.

claims.claim: gthread workers are the cheapest way to get more headroom if near capacity, well before gevent
claims.measured: I/O wait: flask sync 276 req/s, flask-gthread 374 req/s, flask-gevent 2,956 req/s
claims.why: gthread did beat sync Flask on waiting workloads (about 1.35x), so the claim points the right way; "cheapest" refers to migration effort, and the gain measured here is small compared with gevent's roughly 10x.

claims.claim: A short insurer timeout plus circuit breaker protects the morning rush more than any change of worker type
claims.measured: I/O wait: flask sync 276 req/s, flask-gevent 2,956 req/s, flask-gthread 374 req/s
claims.why: The benchmark shows gevent handling about 10x more waiting requests than sync, but it never measured a timeout or circuit breaker, so the comparison can't be checked.
